1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5.name: Italian Game: Two Knights Defence, Knight Attack
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5.background: Known since the 17th century: games with it are attributed to Giulio Cesare Polerio and Gioachino Greco. Siegbert Tarrasch called it "bungling".

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 d5.name: Italian Game: Two Knights Defence, Knight Attack, Normal Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 d5.strategy: Blocks the c4-f7 diagonal with a pawn, the soundest way to meet the threat to f7. Black gives up a pawn after exd5 but gets active pieces and time to develop, and with accurate play Black reaches at least equality.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 Bc5.name: Italian Game: Two Knights Defence, Traxler Counterattack
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 Bc5.background: Named after the Czech problemist Karel Traxler, who played it against Reinisch in 1890; in the United States and Britain it is also called the Wilkes-Barre Variation, a name Frank Marshall gave it. No grandmaster has adopted it regularly, though Beliavsky and Shirov have played it in top competition.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 Bc5.strategy: A trap rather than a sound idea: Black ignores f7 and eyes f2, so a greedy Nxf7 runs into ...Bxf2+. But Bxf7+ wins the pawn cleanly, since the knight on g5 guards the bishop and the king must step aside, and White keeps a lasting edge.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 Nxe4.name: Italian Game: Two Knights Defence, Ponziani-Steinitz Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 Nxe4.strategy: Grabs the pawn and ignores f7, but the bishop sacrifice drags the king out and a central pawn push follows, leaving Black's king in the middle and in trouble. An unsound gambit that works only if White does not know the refutation.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 Bc5 5..name: Italian Game: Two Knights Defence, Traxler Counterattack, Bishop Sacrifice Line
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 Bc5 5..strategy: Takes the pawn with check. The knight on g5 guards the bishop, so the king cannot take it back and must move, losing the right to castle. White is a pawn up against a king stuck in the centre, and Black must make quick development and the pressure on f2 count.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 Bc5 5..name: Italian Game: Two Knights Defence, Traxler Counterattack, Knight Sacrifice Line
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 Bc5 5..background: The Traxler Counterattack was first seen in the game J. Reinisch against Karel Traxler at Hostouň in 1890, which went through this position with 5.Nxf7 Bxf2+ and ended in checkmate for Black.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 Bc5 5..strategy: Takes the pawn with a fork on the queen and rook, but ...Bxf2+ drags the king into the open and the complications that follow are about level. White gives up the clear edge that Bxf7+ keeps, for a sharp game in which White's king is the one in danger.

Opens the centre and hits the c5-bishop and the e5 pawn at once, but ...d5 answers immediately against the c4-bishop and the game levels out. Bxf7+ would have won a pawn outright, so this gives away the edge.

The usual answer: the knight on g5 guards the bishop, so the king cannot take it and steps to e7, giving up castling for good. Black is a pawn down with an exposed king, and has to rely on active pieces and the pressure on f2.

Keeps the king off the e-file and sets a trap: if White greedily takes the rook on h8, ...Bg4 and ...Nxe4 turn the attack against White. Black gives up castling just the same and has to rely on the trap and quick development.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 Bc5 5..name: Italian Game: Two Knights Defence, Traxler Variation, Trencianske-Teplice Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 Bc5 5..strategy: Gives the extra pawn back to open the centre: d4 hits the c5-bishop and the e5 pawn, but the bishop on f7 is left held only by the g5 knight. White throws away its edge for a game full of risk.

Pulls the bishop back and keeps the extra pawn, but White's edge is smaller than with the retreat to c4. Black's king is stuck on e7 with castling gone, yet the c5-bishop pressing on f2 gives Black real counterplay. Sound, but it lets some of the advantage slip.

Retreats to the centre, where the e-pawn guards it, and keeps the extra pawn. Black can trade the f6-knight for it, and the recapture exd5 attacks the c6-knight; White keeps the pawn but loses part of the edge. Sound, a little less accurate than the retreat to c4.

Retreats the bishop to c4, so it no longer depends on the g5 knight, and keeps the extra pawn. Black's king is stuck on e7 and cannot castle, so White finishes its development with an edge while Black's play against f2 stays manageable.

The point of the whole line: the bishop takes on f2 with check and drags the white king into the open before the fork on the queen and rook can be used. Black gives a piece for a pawn to gain time and attack the king, and the sacrifice is judged to hold the balance.
Steps the queen out of the fork and attacks the knight, but leaves the rook on h8 to Nxh8. White wins a rook, and Black has to make up for it with an attack on the king.
Grabs a pawn and keeps the f2 sacrifice in reserve, but ignores the fork: Nxd8 takes the queen first, and Black's attack on the exposed king has to prove it is worth a whole queen.

Takes the bishop, the critical test of Black's idea: the king stands exposed on f2 and a knight check follows at once. White is a piece up for the moment but must survive the attack, and the main lines are thought to end level.
Declines the bishop and keeps the king off f2, so ...Nxe4 comes without check. The knight on f7 still forks queen and rook, but the king stays uncastled and Black has lines to open against it.

Steps into the centre instead of capturing the bishop, and ...Nd4+ answers with check at once, bringing a knight into the game with tempo. White ends up taking on f2 anyway, so Black has simply gained a free developing move.

Takes a second pawn with check and keeps the white king in the open. The knight on f7 still hits the queen and rook, but grabbing the rook on h8 can end in mate, so White has to choose the king's square with care while Black brings the queen into the attack.
Castles into a discovered check: the knight on f7 is all that stands between the c4-bishop and the king on g8, so Nxd8+ takes the queen with check.
Saves the queen but leaves the rook on h8 to the knight. White wins the rook, and Black has to make up for it with the attack on the king.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 d5 5.e.strategy: Takes the pawn and ends both threats at once: the d-pawn no longer attacks the bishop or the e4 pawn. White is a pawn up, and Black's compensation is quick development and the initiative rather than material.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 d5 5.B.strategy: Retreats but leaves the e4 pawn to ...Nxe4, which attacks the g5 knight and uncovers the queen's attack on it too. White has to trade the knight off a pawn down, with nothing in return.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 d5 5.d.strategy: Defends both the bishop and the e4 pawn with one move, yet ...dxc4 wins the bishop: after the recapture White has only a pawn for the piece, and the exchange of queens on d1 makes the extra piece count.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 d5 5.e.name: Italian Game: Two Knights Defence, Polerio Defence
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 d5 5.e.background: 5...Na5 has also been called the Chigorin Gambit.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 d5 5.e.strategy: The main line: the knight leaves the pawn's attack with a threat against the bishop, and Black gives up the pawn for lead in development and pressure. The knight stands on the edge of the board for now, but White's extra pawn is hard to hold without care.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 d5 5.e.name: Italian Game: Two Knights Defence, Fritz Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 d5 5.e.background: The German master Alexander Fritz suggested 5...Nd4 to Carl Schlechter, who published analysis of it in the Deutsche Schachzeitung in 1904 and concluded that it was fully viable. P. S. Leonhardt disputed this assessment in 1907.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 d5 5.e.strategy: Moves the knight out of the pawn's attack to a central square instead of regaining the pawn. White stays a pawn ahead, but the knight can be hit by c3 and has few safe retreats, so Black often has to trade or sacrifice it. A sharp game with little margin for error.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 d5 5.e.name: Italian Game: Two Knights Defence, Ulvestad Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 d5 5.e.background: The American master Olav Ulvestad introduced 5...b5 in a 1941 article in Chess Review.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 d5 5.e.strategy: Offers a second pawn to pull the bishop away from d5 and f7. If White takes it, Black wins the d5 pawn back with an attack on the bishop and the g2 pawn. White's precise answer retreats the bishop to f1, and Black is left to prove the compensation.

Regains the pawn at once, but the knight on d5 only blocks the bishop's diagonal for the moment and leaves f7 weak. White can choose between a violent knight sacrifice on f7 and a calm central pawn strike, both hard to meet over the board, so the move is too risky.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 d5 5.e.name: Italian Game: Two Knights Defence, Kloss Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 d5 5.e.strategy: Adds a second attacker on d5, but Black is already a pawn down and the knight on b4 is easily chased away, so there is no clear compensation. White simply plays on with the extra pawn while Black has to hope for tactics.

Counter-intuitive, but the only good answer: the bishop leaves the attacked square and guards g2, so a queen capture on d5 only loses time to a knight development that hits it. White keeps the extra pawn and the pressure on f7 while Black has to prove the compensation.
Takes the pawn, but ...Qxd5 attacks the bishop and the g2 pawn at once, so White loses time defending and the pressure on f7 fades. The game stays level, with Black the easier side to play.
Wins the knight, but ...bxc4 takes the bishop in return, so White's attack on f7 loses its second piece and the advanced c6 pawn is hard to hold. The game is level, and Black has nothing to fear.
Chases the knight, but the sacrifice on f7 refutes it: after the king takes, the d-pawn captures the knight on c6, leaving White two pawns up against an exposed king.

Moves the attacked knight to a square guarded by the e5 pawn, where it defends the b5 pawn and eyes c2. White has to spend time chasing it away, and the game stays sharp and double-edged, with real counterplay for the pawn.

Takes the pawn back with the knight, which also uncovers the queen's attack on the g5 knight, so White must deal with that first. Black rids itself of the cramping pawn and opens the game for its pieces, though White is slightly more comfortable.
Develops with an attack on the queen and eyes a recapture on d5, but f3 answers it at once and the bishop is soon driven off or traded for the knight. White keeps the extra pawn and a lasting edge.

Takes the pawn at once, but Nc3 hits the queen with tempo and drives it off the long diagonal, after which White takes the b5 pawn after all. Black has no threats to show for it. Playable, but it loses time.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 d5 5.e.name: Italian Game: Two Knights Defence, Polerio Defence, Bishop Check Line
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 d5 5.e.strategy: Moves the bishop out of the knight's attack with check, so no time is lost and the extra pawn stays. Black has to block, and the knight on a5 remains on the edge of the board for now, so White keeps a small edge.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 d5 5.e.name: Italian Game: Two Knights Defence, Polerio Defence, Kieseritzky Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 d5 5.e.background: Paul Morphy preferred this line, which has been named after Lionel Kieseritzky and is also known as the Morphy Variation.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 d5 5.e.strategy: Guards the bishop with a pawn to keep the extra pawn instead of retreating. The cost is that the knight can still trade itself for the bishop, doubling White's c-pawns and giving Black the bishop pair, and Black gets active play for the pawn.

Supports the bishop with the b-pawn instead of retreating. If the knight trades itself for it, the recapture bxc4 doubles White's c-pawns but opens the b-file against Black's queenside; White keeps the extra pawn, Black gets the bishop pair.

The standard block: the pawn attacks the bishop and offers a second pawn. Black gives up material for open lines, a broad centre and active pieces, and plays for long-term pressure while White tries to consolidate the extra pawn.

Blocks the check with the bishop and offers to trade White's active bishop, keeping the pawn structure intact. It is the quieter way to play for the sacrificed pawn: Black gives up the pawn break against the bishop, and with the knight still on the rim, development and open lines must pay for the pawn.

Blocks with the f6 knight, but White simply trades it off with the check. Black loses the piece that eyes d5 and covers the kingside, leaves the other knight on the rim and still faces the knight on g5 aiming at f7: a pawn down with little to show for it.
Questions the knight that has only just come to g5: it must go back, undoing the time White spent attacking f7, and Black gains a tempo. Black gets good chances for the pawn.

Trades the offside knight for White's bishop at once, which removes the piece aimed at f7 and leaves Black the bishop pair. White recaptures with the d-pawn, doubling the c-pawns, but keeps the extra pawn, and the knight on g5 stays unchallenged, so Black has little to show for the pawn yet.
Hangs the queen: the bishop on c4 takes it, and the knight's recapture leaves Black with a bishop for the queen.

Hits the knight with a pawn at once: its retreat squares are poor, so Black must trade it or sacrifice it. White keeps the extra pawn and the pressure on f7, while Black needs active play to justify the pawn.

Defends the extra pawn with a developing move instead of challenging the knight on d4. White keeps the pawn, but Black's central knight stays put and the knight on g5 can be harried, so the game stays unclear and Black's pieces are active.

Gives the extra pawn back at once. After ...Qxd6 the f7 pawn is attacked twice and guarded by the king alone, but Black's knight stays strong on d4 and Black has good play. A playable way to fight for the initiative, without keeping the pawn.

Answers the attack on the knight with an attack on the bishop: if White simply takes the knight, Black takes the bishop, a trade that removes a key attacker of f7. White keeps the extra pawn but must now retreat the bishop.

Retreats the attacked knight to f5 instead of letting it be traded on d4. Black keeps all the pieces but loses time, and White, a pawn up with bishop and knight still aimed at f7, keeps the initiative.

Counter-attacks the knight on g5 while Black's own knight on d4 hangs to the c-pawn, so both knights are attacked and a trade of knights follows. Black plays for activity against the extra pawn, but White keeps the pawn and the pressure on f7.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 d5 5.e.name: Italian Game: Two Knights Defence, Lolli Attack
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 d5 5.e.background: Bobby Fischer thought the Lolli Attack, 6.d4, very strong.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 d5 5.e.strategy: Takes the centre and attacks e5 while keeping the pressure on f7: the knight on d5 is the only piece standing between the bishop and f7. A good, safer alternative to the sacrifice, giving White a lasting edge without its complications.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 d5 5.e.name: Italian Game: Two Knights Defence, Fried Liver Attack
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 d5 5.e.background: Also called the Fegatello Attack, after an Italian dish. It has been known for many centuries, the earliest known example being a game played by Giulio Cesare Polerio before 1606.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 d5 5.e.strategy: The knight sacrifices itself to drag the king into the open: it forks queen and rook, and after the king takes, a queen check chases it to the middle of the board. White gets a fierce initiative for the piece, and defending is much harder than attacking.
Retreats the attacked knight to the centre, but ...f5 kicks it away at once. White gives up the attack on f7, so Black develops without difficulty, and the early knight moves have gained nothing.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 d5 5.e.name: Italian Game: Two Knights Defence, Pincus Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 d5 5.e.strategy: Checks first so that the bishop can return to e7 hitting the g5 knight, but c3 blocks the check for free, and after the return Nxf7 and Qf3+ drag the king into the open. The check wins no time.

Takes the second central pawn and opens the e-file, with the strong knight on d5 intact. But White castles, brings the rook to the e-file and attacks f7 with the g5 knight, so the extra pawn is hard to keep and the king is under fire.

Covers f7 and supports the d5 knight, and invites the knight trade on e6 that opens the f-file for Black at the price of doubled e-pawns. It is the solid way to meet the attack, but White keeps a lasting edge in the centre.

Takes the pawn with the c6-knight instead of the e-pawn, so the e-pawn stays on e5 and the d5 knight keeps its central post. White's c3 challenges the knight at once, but Black can answer by hitting the bishop, and the game stays level.

Forced, since the knight on f7 forks the queen and rook. Black wins a piece for a pawn, but the king is dragged to the centre, and the queen check that follows decides whether Black can survive the attack.
Steps out of the fork but leaves the rook on h8 attacked and the knight on d5 unprotected: 7.Nxh8 wins the rook, and the bishop on c4 also threatens the knight.
Attacks the knight with the king, but the knight takes the queen first: 7.Nxd8 wins the queen for a knight.
